<translation>
<pb n="232"/>The second chapter. When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "O Son of the Conqueror, oh, this assembly is utterly pure; these are Bodhisattvas who have perfectly purified their superior intention, perfectly purified their conceptual thinking, perfectly practiced what is to be practiced, made offerings to many billions of Buddhas, perfectly accumulated the collections, are endowed with immeasurable qualities, are free from hesitation and doubt, are without afflictions, are well-established in superior intention and conviction, and are a gathering consisting entirely of those who are not dependent on others regarding these Buddha-dharma." Therefore, regarding the statement: "O Son of the Conqueror, since these Bodhisattvas are entirely those who abide in this state through direct perception, please explain it well," why did the noble Vimukticandra praise that assembly? It was to show that "even if such individuals are rare in the world, they are present in this assembly." In that regard, "perfectly purified superior intention" is a branch. That perfectly purified superior intention should be understood as twofold: purity of transmission and purity of realization. In that regard, purity of transmission is also fivefold: for the purpose of conceptualizing the means to obtain the desired transmission, purity of aspiration is what is meant by "perfectly purified conceptual thinking." Purity of seeking by engaging in conduct of body and speech consistent with obtaining that is what is meant by "perfect practiced what is to be practiced." Purity of retention by holding many undistorted teachings for a long time is what is meant by "made offerings to many billions of Buddhas." Purity of what is obtained through birth, because one obtains a distinction of mindfulness due to being especially exalted in successive lifetimes through the distinction of one's prayers, is what is meant by <pb n="233"/>"perfectly accumulated the collections." Purity of application by being endowed with many qualities such as having few desires while seeking what is virtuous in the effort to comprehend is what is meant by "endowed with immeasurable qualities." Purity of realization is fourfold: purity of thorough realization because of being perfectly certain through direct knowledge is what is meant by "free from hesitation and doubt." Purity of the non-movement of afflictions, because no secondary afflictions arise on the path of meditation, is what is meant by "without afflictions." Purity of not being content, because one does not desire the Lesser Vehicle but desires to obtain the higher distinctions, is what is meant by "well-established in superior intention and conviction." In that regard, "superior intention" is faith and aspiration. "Conviction" is holding the objects of those as qualities. Purity of being independent of others regarding instructions and teachings, because one has correctly entered by oneself into the movement toward the final goal, is what is meant by "not dependent on others regarding these Buddha-dharma." Vajragarbha said: "O Son of the Conqueror, this assembly is indeed composed of perfectly pure Bodhisattvas who have perfectly purified their superior intention, perfectly purified their conceptual thinking, perfectly practiced what is to be practiced, made offerings to many billions of Buddhas, perfectly accumulated the collections, are endowed with immeasurable qualities, are free from hesitation and doubt, are without afflictions, are well-established in superior intention and conviction, and are a gathering consisting entirely of those who are not dependent on others regarding these Buddha-dharma. However, if others were to hear such an inconceivable state as this, and having heard it, hesitation and doubt were to arise, it would be of no benefit to them for a long time <pb n="234"/> and would lead to harm and unhappiness; thus, out of compassion, I am inclined to remain silent." This refers to how the noble Vajragarbha accepted the purity of that assembly, yet by saying "if hesitation and doubt were to arise after hearing," he shows the fault of not being a vessel for this teaching. Because two types of faults regarding a single object are present, he showed them as two: "hesitation" and "doubt." These two are inconsistent with straightforward action. It is "doubt" because there is suspicion in the mind and because it removes virtue by causing it to decline. Thus, he has fully shown the cause for not proceeding and the cause for turning back from proceeding. Then, for that very same reason, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra again requested the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: "O Son of the Conqueror, please explain it well; by the power of the Tathagata, such inconceivable states as these will be perfectly protected and will also become objects of trust. Why is that? O Son of the Conqueror, this is the reality <note>original: "dharmata"</note> obtained when this explanation of the grounds is spoken: here, all Buddhas will turn their intention toward it, and all Bodhisattvas also strive to protect this very ground of wisdom. Why is that? O Son of the Conqueror, this is the primary practice, because it is for the sake of correctly accomplishing the Buddha-dharma. O Son of the Conqueror, it is like this: for example, that which precedes all syllables, letters, and the teaching of numbers is the alphabet <note>literally: "mother of letters"</note>, and that which brings them to completion is also the alphabet; whatever written letters, syllables, and teachings of numbers there are, none can be shown without the alphabet. O Son of the Conqueror, likewise, since all Buddha-dharma are accomplished through practice, those grounds are the precursor. Because they result in the culmination of the self-arisen primordial wisdom, they are the completion. Therefore, O Son of the Conqueror, speak, and the Tathagatas..."
</translation>
<summary>The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra requests Vajragarbha to teach the grounds of realization, highlighting the purity and readiness of the assembled Bodhisattvas. Vajragarbha initially hesitates out of compassion for those who might doubt the profound teaching, but Vimukticandra emphasizes that the grounds are the essential foundation for all Buddha-dharma, likened to an alphabet.</summary>
<keywords>Vimukticandra, Vajragarbha, Bodhisattva grounds, purity of intention, alphabet analogy, doubt, Tathagata, primordial wisdom</keywords>
